title: A professional project structure
idea: A professional structure gives each kind of file its own folder under `src/`, so you can guess where any piece of code lives.
points: `routes/` maps URLs to handlers; `controllers/` holds the handlers.
`models/` defines the data; `db/` opens the MongoDB connection.
`middlewares/` and `validators/` hold checks that run before a handler.
`utils/` holds shared helpers; `constants.js` holds fixed values.

steps.caption: `index.js` is the entry point: the file you start with `node`. It imports `db/` and `app.js`.
A route lists its checks first, then its handler: `middlewares/` before `controllers/`.
Middleware and controllers reach data through `models/`. Controllers also use helpers from `utils/`.
Arrows never point back: a model never imports a controller.

code.title: Lay out the project
code.caption: Run it in an empty folder. Every file starts empty; each lesson fills in one.

walk.text: Create the project folder and move into it.
`mkdir -p` creates every folder at once; `{a,b}` expands to each name.
`touch` creates an empty file for each name, so the layout exists before the code.
`find` lists every file; `sort` fixes the order.

pitfalls: Never import upward. A model that imports a controller creates a circular import.
Match the lecture's file names exactly, such as `user.models.js`; later imports depend on them.
Keep `utils/` for shared helpers. Request handling belongs in controllers.

quiz.q: Which import breaks the one-way rule?
quiz.why: Imports run from routes down to models. A model that imports a controller points back up and forms a cycle.

takeaway: Group files by role, and let imports point one way: down.

starters: Should I group files by feature instead of by role?
